subsystems.name: Quantum processor
subsystems.role: the hardware that runs the circuits — today noisy, with tens to hundreds of physical qubits.

subsystems.name: Data encoding
subsystems.role: loads information into quantum states, the step that decides whether a speedup is even possible.

subsystems.name: Parameterised circuit (ansatz)
subsystems.role: the trainable model — layers of gates whose angles are the learnable weights.

subsystems.name: Measurement and readout
subsystems.role: turns a quantum state into numbers a classical computer can use.

subsystems.name: Classical training loop
subsystems.role: adjusts circuit parameters to reduce a cost function.
parts: gradient estimators such as the parameter-shift rule
frameworks such as Qiskit, Cirq or PennyLane

subsystems.name: Error handling
subsystems.role: keeps noisy results usable, or corrects them as hardware improves.

buildSteps.title: Decide whether quantum helps
buildSteps.detail: Check if the data is genuinely quantum, or has structure a quantum model exploits — otherwise a classical method is usually cheaper and better.

buildSteps.title: Encode the data
buildSteps.detail: Map each input sample onto a quantum state using rotations or amplitudes; this loading step is often the hidden bottleneck.

buildSteps.title: Design the ansatz
buildSteps.detail: Choose a circuit template with tunable gate angles and enough entangling layers to represent the target function.

buildSteps.title: Define the cost function
buildSteps.detail: Pick an observable whose measured expectation value scores how well the model is doing.

buildSteps.title: Estimate gradients
buildSteps.detail: Run the circuit many times per parameter to estimate gradients, using the parameter-shift rule or similar methods.

buildSteps.title: Train with a classical optimiser
buildSteps.detail: Feed the estimates to a classical optimiser, update angles, and repeat — watching for barren plateaus where gradients vanish.

buildSteps.title: Apply error mitigation
buildSteps.detail: Correct for hardware noise by running calibration circuits and extrapolating, or by zero-noise techniques.

buildSteps.title: Benchmark against classical models
buildSteps.detail: Compare on identical data against strong classical baselines; a claimed advantage only counts if it survives this test.

buildSteps.title: Scale to fault-tolerant hardware
buildSteps.detail: For provable advantages, run the algorithm on error-corrected logical qubits — a step that does not yet exist.

prerequisites.why: most proven quantum speedups assume fault-tolerant circuits; today's devices are too noisy.
loading classical data into a quantum state can cost more than the speedup it enables.
gradients in many ansatz designs shrink exponentially with size, stalling training.
quantum sensors and simulators do produce genuinely quantum data, the clearest near-term use case.
neural networks are cheap and effective, so any quantum claim must beat them, not just match them.

pathway.milestone: small-scale experiments on noisy hardware, mostly learning properties of quantum states
pathway.unlocks: tooling and intuition, but no demonstrated broad advantage.

pathway.milestone: provable advantages on quantum data from sensors or simulators, with error mitigation
pathway.unlocks: a real, narrow commercial niche before general speedups.
larger circuits where quantum kernels and linear-algebra routines start to pay off.

pathway.milestone: fault-tolerant quantum models for chemistry, materials and possibly classical data
pathway.unlocks: speedups on problems classical machines handle poorly — if data loading is ever solved.
